segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s like that everywhere.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Yeah, it’s like that everywhere. The children are not there…

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, it’s hard to bring them now… We’re going to talk for a little while. They got it written down here what I’m supposed to ask you all.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It wasn’t just me.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: You didn’t plan it yourself?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: No, no, no. And if you all don’t like it, it was the one sitting here. All you have to say is “awadetlesd(i)” – “it’s a secret.” If you don’t want to [say something], you don’t have to. But I’m not going to ask you anything about secrets, it’s just going to be something important is what I’m going to be asking about. Starting out, what is your name in English?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: In English? Weynema Smith.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Weynema Smith. And you?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Wanda Robertson.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Wanda Webberson.

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Robertson.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh! Robertson. What about in Cherokee, what is your name?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Tsigeyu.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Tsigeyu. Who gave you that, your Cherokee name?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: It was my grandmother. We were orphaned by her daughter, she was our mom. They took us in and that is where we grew up. There were three of us: my brother, sister, and me.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And what about you? What’s your Cherokee name?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Ganeda.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Ganeda. And who named you, Ganeda?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: It was my mom.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You got her name from way back, like the people that were here long ago.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: My grandfather, his second cousin, he had a name like that. It is a real old name. He said, “I want to name her that.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So that’s where you all got it? I remember now. That’s what happens now, they pass down names from a long time ago. Sometimes, they get them from the Bible, that’s what they name you. Where … What year were you born, and also, where were you born?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: 1932 was the year.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: May 13th.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: OK. And where were you born?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Near Tsisgvnvgesdv – Notchitown, they call it. It’s a community. My grandfather had land there, that was given to him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And that’s where you were born?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Some are not born in the hospital. Just at home. A long time ago, there were women that knew that kind of work. They would go get them.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: My grandmother used to do that. Sometimes they’d call her from way off and she would go.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: She probably stayed until it was all over.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And what about you? Where were you born and what year was it?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: It was there, wasn’t it? Same place. Notchitown, ain’t it? 1949.

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: I don’t know my numbers in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: I just know to 10.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: OK. So you were born at home?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s a good place to start. You don’t have to leave the home, like some are born in the hospital and that’s where they come from. It’d probably be good if we all were born at home. Me too, I was born at home. But today, it’s under water.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Is it toward Jay?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, it’s a place called Old Eucha, they call it. I don’t know if you’ve heard of it. Old Eucha.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Huh-uh, I haven’t heard of it. Me too, where I grew up is under water now. What they call Tenkiller Lake. That’s where we moved from, a whole lot of Cherokees.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Us too, that’s how it was. There were a lot of Cherokees living in Old Eucha. They had a lot of corn fields, it was real pretty. They plowed them all the time. There was a dam and…how do you say monkey in Cherokee?…

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Adalesgiyisgi.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Adalesgiyisgi… they had monkeys in it.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: They had them in there?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah! And also, they had big cats in there in the dam on the rocks. It was made real good, the dam. There were steps, to go down there in the dam. And when it dried up, you could see those steps there. It was good. And what about you? Where did you grow up? Just there at home?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So she’s the one that got after you all the time, the one sitting here?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Yeah!

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: The man I married, we found each other in Marble City. And that’s where I moved to. He was a farmer, he had big plots.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So that’s what drew you to him?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Yeah. Do you know? We only had one child, this one sitting here.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Marble City, you mentioned. Where I’m from there was a family that left and came to Marble. And their name was Cheater.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Oh yeah!

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They left from there and came to Marble City. It was a long time ago.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: And they are still there. The younger generation.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah. The Cheaters. That is where they came from. And what about you? Where did you work at? Did you work anywhere?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: I would get hired to work a bunch of different places. The store in Cookson that was there, I worked there for nine years. There, and Northeastern, I worked there for a few years.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess it was a good place to work, Northeastern?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Yeah, it was real good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And what about you? Where did you work?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Not really anywhere.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: No? … She was the one that had you working?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How many children do you have? You said this is the only one.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Yeah, this is the only one.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How about your siblings? Are there still some? How many were there?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: It’s just me now. They’re already gone.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They’re gone.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: My brother, his name was Saliguwi. And my sister’s name was Oni, she was the oldest. That is one of the old names, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where did they get that?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: My grandfather named her. They were already old when we came to live with them. So, they’re not here, my brother and sister. It’s just me.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Just you.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: My parents, too. It’s been a long time since…

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: …they left.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: I think I was about five or six when my mom passed away. My dad, too, it’s been several years since he passed. His parents were already gone, so everybody’s just gone already. That Notchitown I mentioned, it’s a little community. He had been given land, my grandfather. He gave 10 acres where he wanted a church built. He wanted all his grandkids to go to school there. Even today, they still have the church there. And he’s been gone a long time.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What’s that church called?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Cedar Springs.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Cedar Springs.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Baptist Church.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Cedar Springs, where’s that at?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Where the dam is, past there, about nine miles from there. If you’re going to Notchitown – Tsisgvnvgesdv, that’s where it is.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Gore.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Yeah, they call it Gore.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I’m the pastor at Kenwood Church.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Oh, really?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. It’s called Steeley. I’ve been there for a few years.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They haven’t run me off yet.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It might happen soon.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There were a lot of old people when me and my wife came. Then they all started leaving. It was built back around 1930. I don’t know if you remember the CPA that was here…?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Oh yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They’re the ones who built it, out of rock. But they built us a new church. It was about 2013 when we moved into it. Then it got too small [for us]. The older rock building is still here, a lot of people come just to take pictures of it. But they don’t want me to go stand by it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: My dad, he used to do that, lay down rocks. It’s still there, the Gore High School building. He’s one of the ones who helped build it with rocks. [Made of rock]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What the older people were talking about at Steeley, they were cutting the rocks into 3 or 4 inches. And they had to carry them back to put them on the building (lay them).

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: They sure were working hard, weren’t they?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, they were working hard.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: They didn’t have anything that was easy work.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: No, not back then. They were changing shifts. They would work two or three days and then different ones would come. That’s what they would do to find a little money to live on. They would change shifts.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: That’s right, they did work.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They worked hard back then.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: You know they did. My husband and his brother, when they were out of season with their farming in the fall, then they would go to Colorado…

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, is that where they were going?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: …yeah, to find money to live on. He would go for about six weeks and then come home. What year was it? It was about 15 years ago. The others started talking to him about Tenkiller Lake filling up. And the people were buying land to build houses by the lake. They were telling him he could probably find a good job there. That was when we moved and he found a job laying rocks.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And what about you? You didn’t work anywhere?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. How many children do you have?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Three.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Three.

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Girls.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They’re all girls?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess they’re the ones that helped you out all the time?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s right.

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: [Laughter]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You didn’t have to wash dishes, did you?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah. Yeah, some of the girls can be good workers once they learn. And they really need to learn.

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: They really should.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: If they get married, they might find a lazy man.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They would pick a lazy woman and they don’t want the one that will work. What about your parents, what were their names? Or the ones who raised you? Or your parents – what were their names?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: My grandpa’s name was Galogwed(i) Locust. John Locust was his name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: John Locust.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: His wife’s name was Wadi.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Wadi.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: They only had one child, a girl. And that was our mom. She was only 26 when she died of a disease. And they hardly ever went to the doctor. They just used their medicine from the woods. It didn’t help her. So…the three of us were orphaned. That was it, the old woman. The Locusts. On my dad’s side, they’re Webbers.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Webber.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: That town they call, Tsun(a)sdal(i) – Webber Falls. That’s who it’s named after, my grandfather.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: When they left, they left before the Trail of Tears. They were being removed from their homes. So they said, “Let’s just leave. ‘Cause that’s what’s going to happen to us.” They didn’t want to go. But very few of them came with them. They lived in Russellville for a while. They were doing real well there; farming and tilling. And they would have plots for corn. But, just like they are, the White people — I don’t really like to talk about them — but they were the ones that were taking over their land, ‘cause they could see how well they were doing raising corn. That’s how we Cherokees are, we don’t want to do anything about it. They just said, “Let’s just leave.” When they left, they followed the Arkansas River and that’s how they ended up in They just said, “Let’s just leave.” When they left, they followed the Arkansas River, and that’s how they ended up in… Webber Falls. They made a store there. “If I have a store, maybe I can help the Cherokees that are coming off the Trail,” he said. “The others are charging them too much for the food they are selling to them,” he said. And that’s what he did, he opened up a store in Webber Falls. They got the word “falls” because there were waterfalls in the river somewhere. But you can’t see them today.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Do you know where they were? The waterfall?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: What is it?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: The waterfall that was there. Do you know whereabouts it was in the river?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Oh. Huh-uh, I didn’t see them myself.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I’ve only heard of it.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: They had already tore them down, the Corps of Engineering.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: People were plowing the ground there by the river. I didn’t see them, but my brother did. Because he was way older than me. He saw those falls, they say.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They really had a hard time when they left North Carolina.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: They really, really did. I guess they really looked up to God to get them through, cause they made it here. Do you know that song, “One Drop of Blood?”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: The first words in that song are, “What can I do for you?” they ask Jesus. “What can we do for you, Jesus?” They thought there was still something they could do to help people, they were thinking. But that’s not what it was. That’s what they said. And that was what our grandpa was teaching us. They didn’t have electricity back then. We just had kerosene lamps in our houses. In the wintertime, at about midnight, that’s when he liked to tell stories. What they did as they were growing up. I’ve learned a whole lot from those old people.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really. Our parents that were growing up way, way back—we didn’t know that they were having hard times.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: We didn’t.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We didn’t realize it.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: We didn’t. And they didn’t tell us either.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: No. They were just always laughing around. I remember, like you said—I remember the first house we lived in—or stayed with (someone). Back then, people could live with somebody without problems.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Huh-uh, no.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Also, they didn’t really care. Also, back then, they visited each other a lot.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: They really did.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: But it’s not like that today. Back then, they just cooked on the ground. There wasn’t a place to cook (kitchen).

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: That’s how it was where everybody lived.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When it was winter, the ground was really warm where the fire was. They would sweep it.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: It wasn’t dusty either. It was already coals.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s right. I think about it sometimes—I go back then when I’m thinking about it.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Me too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Also, no matter how much a Cherokee owes somebody, they’ll still be laughing around. A white person just hangs his head down, thinking about it. Your parents, where they lived, that’s where you grew up?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Yeah, it was there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s where they grew up.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: My grandpa used to work here and there. Wherever he got hired. He was working for the white people. The farmers hired him. That’s where Mom and Dad met. His dad, his parents gave them some land to build on. That’s where we were born, us children.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Your mother was Cherokee?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Yes, she was a good Cherokee speaker. They were all speakers. That’s all they spoke back then, Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s right. That’s all they spoke back then.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: My dad, he understood Cherokee. But they [his family] spoke Creek. My brother and I, we spoke [Creek] for a while, until we were five or six. Then Cherokee got in the way. Then, when we started school, we learned English. [laughs] We forgot it [Creek].

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s really how it was.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about, what is your clan? What they call ‘clan.’

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Ahawi – Deer.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Ahawi.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Deer Clan.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And you? The same? You’re in the Deer Clan?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: My husband was in the Wolf Clan.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Wolf Clan.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: They didn’t allow for the same clans to marry.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. As I was growing up, when I talked to a girl they always told me she was my cousin. [laughs] Is that what they said to you?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Yeah. My husband’s brother says, he finished 27 years in the service. He got drafted to start with—but he stayed that many years. He got a German woman there. “That’s all I knew to do cause when I went with a girl here, they always said she was a cousin,” he said.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He went and got one overseas. [laughs]

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Yeah. He went and found one there overseas.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about your parents, where did they meet?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Right there at Notchitown. Where my grandpa had given him land. Or, enisi, you’d say. Cause it was my dad’s…his parents. This is the old way of saying ‘eduda.’ If it’s our mom’s, ‘tsugayvlige’ that’s what you say. If it’s our dad, ‘enisi’ you say. They’re different.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, they’re different.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: That’s where they were, ‘cause they had already given them land with houses on it. He already had a church going, too. So they gave my dad land to build him a house to raise kids when he got married. That’s where we grew up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about you? Where did you and your husband meet?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: It was in Marble City. [laughs]

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Yeah. I started to say Sallisaw, but it was in Marble (City).

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So you found each other in Marble City. What does your husband do?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: He passed away.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He passed away? Well, I’ll be.

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: He was a white man.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He was white.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: He was just about a quarter Cherokee.

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, well, I’ll be.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: What was his name? … What was his name?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Sam.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Sam?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Robertson.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sam Robertson … Your last name…

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Do you mean ‘maiden’ name?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Webber.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Webber. That name Webber, you say, is why they named the town, Webber Falls.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: That’s what they say.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s what they say. What do you think is the reason they gave it that name?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Like I was saying, when they left Arkansas, they were following the Arkansas River and they arrived there. They were having a hard time from the Trail of Tears. “They didn’t have nothing. They didn’t have any food,” he (her grandpa) said. He decided to open a store. “I can sell things cheaper and help them that way,” he said. That was my grandpa. And that’s what he did, he built him a store. That’s where the Cherokees shopped. That was how they named the town Webber Falls.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They did good in naming the town that.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Uh-huh. Really, for sure.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He was the very first one to have a store there.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: The very first. There was nothing, it was just a wooded area. There was water running nearby, they call it the Arkansas River.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They really did good when they named the town Webber Falls.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Really, it was.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do the ones living in Webber Falls know where its name came from?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: No, they don’t really know.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They don’t really know what all happened why it’s named that.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Why it’s named that. Even my family doesn’t really know what all happened before it became a town named Webber Falls. They said the waterfalls were falling.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And you, when you were in school, is that where you went in Webber Falls?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Huh-uh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: No?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Huh-uh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: You started school at Marble (City) right?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Yeah, Marble (City).

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You started at Marble (City).

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: My husband started looking for a job in Cookson. That’s where we moved to and they had a school. That’s when she started going to school there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess you learned a lot there?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Yeah. [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s where you and your husband found each other?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Uh-huh.…Marble (City).

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It was Marble (City), yeah. What year was it when that bridge at Marble (City) tore up? What year was it?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Hold on… Probably about in the ‘40s.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is that when it was? That bridge that was by Marble (City), on the other side, it tore up.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Oh. They fixed it. It didn’t really tear up, ‘cause they fixed it. They ‘extended’ it, you’d say. Gah-lee, it’s been a long time ago.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Yeah, it’s been a long time ago now.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: It was probably around the ‘30s.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, I heard that it had happened. They said some people fell into the water with their wagons.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: They didn’t have those…what would you say?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Siderails.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: It was just flat.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Yeah, it was just a flat bridge. That’s why they were falling off. The water current was too strong for some of them. That’s just how it was.

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: I remember that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. I heard that that had happened.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Uh-huh. Really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: “Their bridge at Marble (City) tore up,” they said.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Uh-huh, yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What did you say your Cherokee name was?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Tsigeyu.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Tsigeyu. And you?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Ganed(a).

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Ganed(a). So they had never given you a nickname? My name is Richard, but they call me Guy. I don’t know where they got “Guy.” There were a lot of people, they were giving them nicknames. Did they ever give y’all a name? They call it a nickname. They didn’t ever give y’all a nickname?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Huh-uh. Not really. My husband, his Cherokee name was Igayihe. But nobody called him that. They called him Tike.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Tike. That’s the nickname they gave him.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: They said he was a drummer (stompdance), they said. He was a great Creek stompdance leader . And they said he liked listening to stompdance. He would mimic the songs, that’s how he learned to sing. That’s how he got his nickname. ‘Tike,’ they called him.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How about you? Do you have a--?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Huh-uh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So whatever they called you, that what it was?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s it.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: My grandkids... My great-grandkids, they’re twins, a girl and a boy. They are going to school here, learning Cherokee. They were only three years old when they started. They’re four now. They are in Norman somewhere. They are performing what they have learned. The teachers gave him the name Ganed(a).

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is it Ganedi?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: The same name as her (Wanda).

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: And they’re really learning Cherokee well.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s good.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: I’m really proud of them. I really wanted them to learn Cherokee. “Don’t lose the language,” they used to tell us as we were growing up. I started teaching when I was about 20 years old. I’ve been teaching here and there since. If they wanted to gather up somewhere, like at a church, I would teach them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Zeb. They probably know each other.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: And he’s teaching now. He came to live with me, my grandson. We were talking Cherokee all the time. We used to sit around until midnight, just talking. He was hearing it (Cherokee) and he thought it sounded good. “I wonder what they are saying,” he thought. (…) He had already graduated high school. He was also going to college at that time. All of a sudden, he started learning Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Yeah, he finished. He graduated. And all of a sudden, he was called to be a teacher. He’s been teaching Cherokee language since. We call him ‘Zeb’, his name is Zebadiah. He’s slender and tall. I think he teaches sixth graders.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Here?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well, I’ll be.

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Zeb Nofire.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Nofire is his last name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Nuwotvn(a) is his name.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What was his name?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Zeb.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Deb?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Zeb.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Zeb.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Zeb Nofire.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Zeb Nofire.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: We call him Zeb, you know, like his nickname.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: A lot of people just know him by Zeb. Zebadiah is his name. Zeb, that’s his nickname.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, Zebadiah.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: He really wants to learn. He stayed right in there with them, teaching.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He really wants to teach them. That’s really good for him to be a teacher.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: It really is.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Some think they just have to do it. But if the teacher really wants them to learn, they’re going to learn.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There’s a difference in a teacher thinking, “I have to do this,” and a teacher that really wants to teach.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Very much so. I was surprised that he’s doing that. Because I never told him he should go teach the Cherokee language. He was staying with me. When he finished Northeastern, he saw it online somewhere that they were hiring for a Cherokee language teacher.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: That’s when they called him, and he’s been teaching since.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s good what he’s doing. A few nights ago, a white man came to visit. He also saw something online. And today, he speaks Cherokee. He speaks real good. He’s white, too, not part Cherokee.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Ooh!

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: He came from Chicago, Illinois.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: He saw some people speaking Cherokee somewhere. He was amazed. “I really want to learn that,” he said to himself. Gah, he speaks the whole language real well.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Weynema Smith &

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Ooh!

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Way better than me. [laughs]

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: That’s like what you said: if they really want to learn, they learn.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s what will happen. We all had a great conversation with him for a while.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I didn’t really think he was a white man. I thought he might be mixed with something else. [laughs] He spoke real well.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: That’s great. Does he teach somewhere?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I don’t think so. Right?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Not yet?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: He was helping a college professor. At Oklahoma University, I think.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Oh!

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I think.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: That is the highest school where they are teaching Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. What about when you all were growing up? Did they talk about important things or things they saw?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: I don’t remember.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: They didn’t really talk about things like that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Some people talk about Little People. Or ghosts. They didn’t talk about things like that?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Hmm, not that much. The soldiers, they’re warm (southerners), they called them. They said they were bothering them a lot, because they didn’t have a man. They were fighting in a war, Grandma was saying. She would tell it. Someone came and told them, “They are coming. Just be ready to hide.” “It was just us women there,” she said. “Three or four of us women,” she said. “We were all helping each other, living together. One of the women’s dad, he was really old, also sickly. He started worrying about it. ‘What am I going to do?’ He was crippled. He was crying. They told him, ‘Do not cry. If the others see you crying, they’re going to know something is wrong,’ they told him. ‘Don’t be crying,’ they told him. ‘Let’s just look for something to keep us strong. Let’s just hide him,’ they said. There was a cellar there. They were storing potatoes in there, and the hole was smaller because of that. So they wrapped him up, the old man. We had him laying flat on the ground. The women were outside there. They were just sweeping around when they came. They ran around all over the place looking for some things to take. Our plan worked, hiding the old man.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, he got away, didn’t he?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: They were really mean, she said. But they were in need of things. When we bought new shoes, we had to hide them in the woods, she said. We couldn’t keep the shoes in the house. When the mean people came, they would take the shoes. All the things that they could use, they would take it all from us, she said. I guess they grew up being poor. They were saving things they needed to use at home.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s true. You talked about, awhile ago, about the people that came from North Carolina. Did they all come to Webber Falls? Or did they just go everywhere when they got there?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: No. They just all stayed around there. Families stayed together.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They all gathered there.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: They were all helping each other. I guess that’s how they had to live, cause there wasn’t any food. They needed a lot of it. Then they were farming and helping each other grow food. They were growing a lot of food. Also, the animals – they were raising cows, pigs, and chickens. Where I grew up, there were a lot of trees – peach, apple, and cherry – that they planted. That is what they used. When they made pies, they used peaches or apples. We would pick them. They were smart to figure out how to preserve things. My grandpa used to grow a lot of turnips. When it was time to pick them, we would help him. He would cut the stems off like this [gestures]. He would get some hay and dig a hole in the ground and put a canopy cloth on the ground to cover the bottom. And then we put the turnips that we had cut in there. All winter we have them down there. We covered them with hay. When they said, “Go get some,” then I would go get some. I would raise up the cover of hay and get some of them out to cook. They just all helped each other. And then the white neighbors would be on the road by our house, just offering things that they have to eat. They’d tell us, “If they need something, just go get it.” Mustard greens, turnips, and spinach were what he had in his garden. It was real pretty. He would offer things to people. Or he would take it to them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And the white people lived the same way. They were also looking for food sometimes. Just like the Cherokees, they were also asking for something to eat. The white people had the same problems.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Yeah, they had the same problems. They said, “If it wasn’t for the Cherokees, we’d probably be all gone. They taught us how to find food.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They were all helping each other, the Cherokees and the white people.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Yeah, everybody was helping each other.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How about you? When you got married, did you make a garden?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Huh-uh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: No?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Things had already changed by that time.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Your husband was feeding you. [laughs]

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: It was that “lime plant” they call it, that’s in Marble. They were the ones that hired you to work. That’s how she got their food. She wasn’t a farmer.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Those places where they work and have big holes with water running, was it really deep? Or were they just saying that?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Huh-uh. It really was deep.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, it was deep.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: The water was coming out. Our family was telling us whereabouts the deep holes were.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They told you all, “Don’t be going over there.”

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: “Don’t be swimming or wading in the water over there,” they’d tell us.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And they talked about snakes being in there. Was it really true?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Mhm. Yeah, it was like that. It was really scary. They would tell us to stay away from there. They would warn us, telling us how dangerous it was over there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is it open or did they close it? In Marble, what we were talking about.

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: It’s still open I think. Right?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh. It has been open there for a long time.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: What we’ve been hearing. I don’t know if we’ve heard the truth. The Cherokee chief we have has bought too much land over there in Marble. That school, where she went to school, they’ve tore it all down. They made it all flat. They’re going to build on it, they said. They said the chief bought it. Some people are always wanting these Mexicans to come here, and they got fences up so they can’t come over here to the United States. Then they were saying they were going to let them come here. But I don’t know if they’re telling the truth or not.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, where I’m from, Jay, they bought the ball field there. From what I hear, they’re going to build houses on it.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s what they’re saying over this way.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Have you all seen these houses here? They are behind the building.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Huh-uh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s the kind of houses they’re going to build.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: They’re just small.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, they’re real small. You’ve seen them, Mitch.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: What is it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: The houses that Cherokee Nation has built. Just behind here.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Oh, just over there?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: My son lives in one.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How big are they?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: They’re real small.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Yeah. My son and his family are in a two-bedroom house. The others, I don’t know, they might be one bedroom. I guess. How big it is, I don’t know. Probably 20…24ft x 40ft, I think. It’s really narrow and long.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s the kind they’re going to build on the land they’re buying.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: That’s what they’re saying about Marble, where they tore the school down. “They’re going to build on it,” they’re saying. There’s another one, where was it? It was Dwight Mission. There, they’re going to bring something in.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Where was it in Dwight Mission? I mean, by the old school or…?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Yeah, there. Dwight Mission buildings are all still there. … The ones they said they’re going to let them come in.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I go by there all the time. I live by Stokes stompground. That’s where I come by, morning and evening. Have you ever been where she’s talking about? Dwight Mission?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I went there a long time ago.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I don’t like to go in there, the school. “Gah!” I thought. This [gestures] happens to me when I go in there.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They say if you’re half-drunk, you really don’t want to go in there.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I would go in there for a while, but then I’d get scared and leave.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: They called me to come to Dwight Mission, and then they told me to tell the people how Dwight Mission came about. When the Webbers got to Russellville, then they had to leave. They decided to come to Webber Falls. He had a lot of logs and boards that he had left over from when he built his own house, and that’s what he gave to Dwight Mission, all the logs and boards for them to build with. That’s what he gave them to use. He really wanted the Cherokees to prosper. “To have schools, so they can get their education,” he said. He wanted Dwight Mission to start a school. That’s how it happened, that they built all those houses because he donated the logs.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Man! Gah-lee. I guess it’s real different since you were growing up, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Oh yeah!

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s not like it was a long time ago.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Nope, it’s not! That’s why they called on me to tell the people how Dwight Mission began. That’s all I know, that my great-great grandpa had given all his logs to them. They tore all his buildings down in Russellville. Then he gave them to Dwight Mission so they’d have a school. That’s what they say.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How about today? Do you think about how it used to be when you were growing up where you were born?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Oh yeah! There’s just a lot to think about. It’s different today, how things have changed. You wouldn’t want to do what they’re doing today. They’re always putting each other down. And they don’t realize it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: No, no.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: They’re all drinking so much. And also, they’re using all kinds of drugs.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s what is crippling their minds a lot.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: That’s what we were saying. When did you say they’re doing surgery on that boy?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Wednesday.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Wednesday. And it’s all because he’s using all those drugs all the time. He’s crippled himself. I think they’re going to do surgery on his kidneys.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, we have raised one boy. He was also doing that; smoking and swallowing some things [drugs]. He was about 19 years old when he left the house, because he didn’t like us getting onto him about that. He was about 30 or 40 when he came back. He had already messed up his mind. He was always hearing and seeing things, and also talking to himself. We tried a few times to get him into rehab, and that was costing us a lot. He would call and say, “I want to come home. Or else, I’m gonna walk back.” We felt sorry for him, and we would go get him, and doing that is why it cost us a lot of money. He was real skinny when he started, but now he’s this [gestures] big. Sometimes… –They told him he will have to take the medicine the rest of his life. And sometimes he will be talking to himself.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: That’s how far he got taking care of himself.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s right. We always warned him, but he didn’t listen.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: No, they won’t listen to a thing you say.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes we would lose things. If we had a little money, then we’d lose that. He would find it and take it.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: After all you had done for him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They don’t care. That’s how they get when they’re using drugs.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: And they bother the family.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, they don’t care about anybody, even their own family, when they get into drugs. If you have little kids, you need to teach them about drugs. It is bad for them to lose control of everything being on drugs. What about what you all were cooking back then? Are they cooking something similar to what you all cooked back then? Like, wild onions, poke salad, and crawdads? Do you all still cook these things?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Oh yeah! We would always go look for them. We get excited in the springtime when it’s time for the onions to grow. Also, poke salad. And then there’s that ‘uganasd(i)’ they call it. And watercress, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I like to eat that. When we got to the house, I would cut it up and put hot grease on it.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: That’s right. I just got hungry.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You’re hungry for that now? You’re going to have to go look for some when you get home. But now, there’s not really…--

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Poke salad is what really helped us. We will live healthier if we keep eating it. And today, we just go to the store.

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Dollar Store.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s why we are always getting sick today.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: That’s right! We don’t know what’s mixed up in our food that we eat.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Even chicken, they say they give them some kind of shots to make them grow fast. Yeah, just like you said, we don’t know what’s mixed in with our food.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Nope! We don’t.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We think we are eating good chicken.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: No telling what’s mixed up into chicken.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Yeah. No, they didn’t go get their food from the store. It was too far to the store, anyway. If you wanted to go get food, it was 20 – 25 miles away. To Gore, from where we lived. They would be gone all day to go get groceries in the wagon.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess they went and got food to last for a month. Like flour.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: That’s right. 50 lbs of flour.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Or 100 lbs of potatoes. It’s a wonder… What did they call them? Those big sacks of potatoes… What did they call them? I forgot. Sometimes, when they ran out of potatoes, when it snowed, they would cut those sacks up and put them on their shoes. We didn’t have snowshoes.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Nope! Just burlap sacks.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They would wrap it on their shoes, the burlap sack, and it would be warm.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: That’s true!

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Today, nobody will do that.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: They’d be ashamed.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They’ll be laughing. Really, they would laugh at you.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Yeah, they’ll laugh at you.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Now we’re about to finish up.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: We could talk all day.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: [laughter]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: This Cherokee language we’re speaking, do you all think it’s going to disappear? Is it going to end?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Yeah, I think it’s going to end.

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about them teaching the language? You think they’re going to learn and use it, or are they just going to forget about it?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: I think so. Because the English language gets in the way. That’s what gets in their way, the English language. They’re going to forget it, Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And what about your kids, do they go to school here?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Huh-uh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: No? Oh, they’re all grown up, right?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Yeah, they’re all grown up.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Where is it that one lives? New Hampshire? Or Maine?

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Maine.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Maine. There isn’t a Cherokee speaker living there, is there?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: No. And they probably don’t understand either. We always spoke Cherokee around them, she used to bring them, those girls, when they were little. And they didn’t learn any of it.

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Huh-uh.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: That is really surprising. If you hear it, you’d think you’d learn it.

segments.speaker: wanda-robertson
segments.translation: Now they want to learn it.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Now they want to learn it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Now that they’ve grown up, they want to learn it. When they were young, they didn’t want to learn it.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Huh-uh. My sister had about six or seven girls. And two boys. Their parents were real good Cherokee speakers, but the kids didn’t learn any of it. That’s real interesting, how that is.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s true. It would be good if we don’t lose it. We don’t know what’s going to happen.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Huh-uh. What is going to happen, they’re going to have to read the Bible, but they don’t know how to speak it. They won’t know what it says in there. That’s what I think.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Also, the writing in Cherokee, they won’t know what it says.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: To interpret it. That’s what I think about all the time.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well I appreciate us talking.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Me too. I really miss having somebody to speak Cherokee to.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah, that’s the way it is.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: There’s hardly anybody who comes to visit me, I live at Cookson.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: Only the white people.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There’s not any Cherokee speakers there?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: A long time ago, there were people named Dirteater living there. Did you all know them?

segments.speaker: weynema-smith
segments.translation: No, I’ve heard of them, but I didn’t know them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, their dad had only one eye. They came from where I’m from.
